issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette: Ravi, a 53-year-old South Asian man, was a painter living in a small town with his wife. He had experienced significant trauma during his time as a civilian in a war zone, an event that had fundamentally altered the way he perceived the world around him. Ravi's traumatic experience involved being caught in the crossfire of gunfire and explosions, which left him feeling helpless and overwhelmed. Ravi’s life since then has been marked by intense triggers and maladaptive coping strategies. The smell of burning rubber or diesel fuel, reminiscent of the war zone, would often bring back vivid memories and plunge him into a state of hypervigilance. Each time he smelled these scents, his body would tense up, ready to react to perceived danger. This response was not just physical; it also triggered intense grief and an overwhelming sense that the world is dangerous. Ravi’s inability to control the situation during the traumatic event had led him to believe that he no longer possessed the capabilities that once defined him as a painter. He felt as though nothing in his life held any meaning anymore, leading him into a cycle of rumination about why this happened to him and an intense need to keep himself busy with other tasks to distract from these thoughts. His hyperalertness extended beyond olfactory triggers; loud bangs or sudden noises would cause him to startle violently. These sounds often brought back the memory of explosions, which made his body reenact the position he was in during those frightening moments. Each time this happened, Ravi felt a profound grief and an unsettling disbelief that such extreme events had actually occurred to him. The sense of loss of control and meaninglessness deeply affected Ravi’s daily life. He found himself avoiding news reports about conflicts or war because they reignited the feelings of vulnerability he experienced during the traumatic event. This avoidance, however, only deepened his negative appraisals that the world is dangerous and that he was no longer capable of doing what once defined him as a painter. Ravi’s coping mechanisms became self-reinforcing: the more he ruminated about why this happened to him, the harder it was for him to engage with his painting. His busyness and avoidance of news reports led him further away from his passion and into a deeper cycle of grief and hypervigilance. He would often find himself working late at night or on weekends, trying to keep his mind occupied and distracted from the memories that haunted him. This self-imposed isolation from his art began to affect his relationships with clients who had come to appreciate Ravi’s unique style and craftsmanship. His wife noticed changes in their daily interactions as well; he was more withdrawn and often preoccupied with thoughts of past events. What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a particularly distressing incident at work where the sound of a hammer hitting nails made him jump violently, causing him to drop his tools and feel an intense wave of grief. He realized that his hypervigilance and avoidance were interfering not just with his personal life but also his professional identity as a painter. Ravi was most afraid of losing control entirely and never being able to find meaning in his work or life again. However, he was hopeful that therapy could help him regain some sense of normalcy and allow him to reconnect with the world around him without feeling constantly on edge. He knew he needed support to break free from the cycles of rumination, avoidance, and hypervigilance that had taken over his life since his traumatic experience.
